summary:
Flame in Freefall is a web dashboard that helps people compare NASA’s microgravity fire experiments with the air conditions of a crew habitat. A user picks Earth, a space station, a Moon base, a rover or a spacesuit. The dashboard then ranks NASA’s test records by how close their oxygen and pressure are to that habitat, shows investigations grouped into prevention, detection and suppression, and displays what NASA has and has not tested for each material. 

Every value links to its NASA source. Short AI explanations and answers are generated only from our records, and each sentence must cite its source, with numbers checked before display. 

The challenge asks for a dashboard that summarises, ranks and interprets this research for crew fire safety, and we address each part. Crewed missions to the Moon and Mars will need fire-safety evidence matched to their own atmospheres, which is often scattered across many experiments. 

Flame in Freefall makes that evidence easier to find, and it shows openly where data is still missing.
details:
Flame in Freefall is a web dashboard that helps someone compare NASA’s microgravity fire experiments against the air conditions of a crew habitat. The user picks a habitat (Earth, Space station, Moon base, Rover or Spacesuit). The dashboard then ranks NASA’s tests by how close their oxygen and pressure are to that habitat, shows which investigations belong to fire-safety groups (Prevent, Detect, Put out) and which are related studies, and shows what NASA has and hasn’t tested for each material.

Each result links to its NASA source. Short AI explanations and answers to questions are generated only from the records we hold. Each sentence must cite a record, and the cited numbers must appear in it. If the check fails, the dashboard shows NASA’s own result text instead.

The pipeline has three parts. A data step downloads NASA’s experiment tables, checks each file against its published hash, and writes them as test records with their source links. A backend (FastAPI, Python) serves the records, rankings, safety table, investigations and checked AI answers. A frontend (React and TypeScript) displays them.

Benefits

  • Engineers and researchers can see which NASA experiments are closest to a given habitat, without reading each one.
  • Every number is traceable to a source, so findings can be checked.
  • Gaps are shown openly: missing tests, missing rules and missing partial-gravity data.

Intended impact

The aim is to make NASA’s fire-safety evidence easier to find and compare for people designing habitats, and to show where the evidence is still missing. The same comparison also supports Earth applications, such as water-mist extinguishers, smoke detectors and firefighter gear, which the dashboard lists with their sources.

Tools and technologies

  • Languages: Python (data build, backend, checks), TypeScript and JavaScript (frontend), HTML and CSS.
  • Backend: FastAPI, Pydantic, Uvicorn, httpx, python-dotenv, pytest, ruff.
  • Frontend: React, Vite.
  • AI: Google Gemini API, for short explanations and answers. Embedding search is used for question retrieval.
  • Data handling: JSON files, CSV parsing, SHA-256 checksums.
  • Development: Git and GitHub, Visual Studio Code, WSL (Ubuntu) on Windows.
  • Hardware: No specialised hardware was needed.

How it is creative

  • It turns many separate NASA experiment tables into one comparison across habitats, which the public PSI interface does not offer.
  • Ranking shows its rule on screen, so anyone can check the calculation.
  • The AI answers are checked against their records before they are shown, and the dashboard openly marks what the check does not verify.
  • Gaps are presented as findings, not hidden: the table shows what NASA has not tested.

Factors the team considered

  • Accuracy: no value is filled in unless a source states it. Missing values stay empty. Habitat values are labelled stated, expected or assumed.
  • Safety wording: the dashboard never describes a material or test as safe or unsafe unless specified.
  • Scope: the team kept 13 of 24 investigations as related studies, rather than forcing them into fire-safety groups.
  • Reproducibility: the data step checks file hashes, and a single check script confirms the data and routes.
  • Limitations: oxygen points and psi count equally in the ranking, so it is a sorting rule, not a flammability model. Partial-gravity data is not yet available.
